Florence, April. Graziella has kept her promise: she is teaching Karl to make ribollita. It's the third lesson, in the trattoria kitchen, at six in the morning. Karl has dared to change something.
What did you put in the soffritto?
A little garlic. Back home in Malta we always put it in.
Garlic in ribollita? My father would turn in his grave.
Don't take it badly, Graziella. I just wanted to try.
I'm not taking it badly. But let me remind you that you're here to learn my recipe, not to invent a new one.
You're right. I was wrong. I'll start again.
Good. And get on with cutting the black cabbage, it's late.

I'm perfectly fine. It's tiredness. At my age it's normal.
I didn't expect that from you. You always say you have to look carefully. And I'm looking at you.

The lessons began on a Monday in April, at six in the morning, when the trattoria was still closed and via Maggio was empty, except for the bread van and a cat asleep on the window sill of Guido's shoemaker's. Graziella had kept her promise, the one made a year earlier, when Karl had left her the note on the kitchen table: "I'm not asking for the two per cent. I'll settle for ninety-eight." There were three rules, and Graziella wrote them on a sheet she pinned above the stove. One: you arrive at six, not at five past. Two: no questions while the cook is tasting. Three: ribollita isn't invented, it's learned. Karl read the rules, nodded and put on an apron. It was the first apron of his life. It was too big for him.

Karl felt at home from the very first day. He liked the early hour, the silence, the smell of the kitchen before the customers arrived, that mixture of wood, oil and yesterday's bread. Above all he liked the way Graziella explained things, without ever really explaining them. She never said "two spoonfuls of oil" or "ten minutes". She said "as much as needed", "until you smell the right smell", "when the onion becomes as transparent as a bridal veil". Karl, who was used to the precise measurements of the spectrometer, went mad at first. Then he understood it was the same method Bellini used with restorers: he didn't give you the rules, he taught you to look. "The recipe isn't in the notebook," Graziella told him on the second day. "It's in your nose. And in your hands. The notebook is only for people who have neither."

On the third morning Karl made the mistake. While Graziella had gone down to the cellar to fetch the beans, he decided to add a clove of garlic to the soffritto, as his mother did in Marsaxlokk with all her soups. It seemed a small improvement. Graziella came back, sniffed the kitchen air like a truffle dog, and stopped in the doorway with the bag of beans in her hand. "What did you put in the soffritto?" she asked in a very calm voice. Karl confessed at once. Graziella put down the bag. For a long moment she said nothing. Then she said only: "Garlic in ribollita. My father would turn in his grave." Karl blushed to the ears and apologised in three languages. "Don't take it badly," he said, "I just wanted to try." Graziella took the pan, threw the soffritto in the bin and gave him a clean one. "I'm not taking it badly," she replied. "But let me remind you that you're here to learn mine. You'll invent yours when you have your own kitchen."

That afternoon, at the workshop, Karl told Chiara about it, convinced Graziella was angry with him. Chiara laughed. "If she'd really taken it badly," she said, "she wouldn't have given you a clean pan. She'd have shown you the door." Then she told him that she too, in her first year, had made a similar mistake: she had cleaned a fifteenth-century panel with a different solvent from the one Bellini had told her to use, because it seemed better to her. Bellini hadn't raised his voice. He had only said: "The day you have your own workshop, you'll use your own solvents. Here we use mine." Karl thought about it. "So Graziella and Bellini are the same," he said. "More or less," replied Chiara. "Except that Bellini, when he forgives you, offers you a coffee. Graziella offers you a bowl of ribollita. And ribollita is better."

That evening Karl phoned his mother, in Malta, and told her about the garlic. He expected her to agree with him, because garlic in soups was her tradition. Instead Mrs Borg laughed so loudly that Karl had to hold the phone away. Then she told him, in Maltese, something he never forgot. She said that when she was young and learning to cook from her mother-in-law, Karl's grandmother, she had once tried putting parsley in the fish broth, and her mother-in-law hadn't spoken to her for three days. "Every kitchen has its laws," she said. "Don't take it badly with Signora Graziella. If she teaches you her laws, it means she considers you family. You feed strangers. You teach family." Karl thought about it all night. The next morning he arrived at five to six, for the first time. Graziella looked at the clock, then at him, and said nothing. But she let him taste the broth.

It was in the fourth week that Karl began to notice things. At first they were small, almost nothing. Graziella, who usually climbed the cellar stairs two at a time, now climbed them slowly, leaning on the wall. In the middle of the morning she would sit on a stool, something she had never done before, and say it was only to keep a better eye on the pot. Once, while lifting the big pot full of broth, she stopped suddenly, with a hand on her chest, and stayed like that for a few seconds, eyes closed. Then she went on stirring as if nothing had happened. Karl, who had learned from Ruggeri and Bellini to observe without touching, said nothing. But that evening he wrote in his notebook, under the recipes, a different list: "Stairs: slow. Stool: every day. Big pot: hand on chest. Complexion: pale."

On the Friday of that week, Karl decided to speak. He waited for Graziella to finish tasting, as rule number two said, then asked her, in the gentlest voice he could find: "Graziella… are you feeling all right? You're pale. And just now, on the stairs, you were short of breath." Graziella turned to him with the ladle in her hand. "I'm perfectly fine," she said. "It's tiredness. At my age it's normal." Karl didn't give up. "I didn't expect that from you," he said. "You always say you have to look carefully. And I'm looking at you." For a moment, something that looked like fear passed through Graziella's eyes. Then it vanished. "Cut the cabbage, Karl," she said, turning back to the stove. "I'll take care of my heart myself." Karl cut the cabbage in silence. But that afternoon, instead of going to the workshop, he went to look for Pietro.

Pietro listened to him sitting on the trattoria steps, with his school rucksack still on his back. When Karl showed him the list in the notebook, he was silent for a long time. Then he said something Karl didn't expect. "I knew," he said. "I didn't want to know, but I knew." He told him that for weeks his grandmother had been falling asleep on the sofa at nine in the evening, with the television on, she who for fifty years had never gone to bed before midnight. That she had stopped going up to the second floor to visit her neighbour. That one morning he had found her sitting in the kitchen, in the dark, with a hand on her chest, and she had told him she was just thinking. "I told myself I was wrong," said Pietro. "That it was me asking too many questions, as usual." He looked at Karl. "But I wasn't wrong, was I?" Karl shook his head. "No," he said. "You were only wrong not to say so sooner."

That night Pietro couldn't sleep. He switched on the computer and looked up his grandmother's symptoms online, one by one: tiredness, shortness of breath, weight on the chest. In half an hour he read so many frightening things that by two in the morning he was convinced Graziella had a month to live at most. He went down to the kitchen for a glass of water and found Karl, asleep on the trattoria sofa because the next day he had to open at five. Karl saw his face and understood at once. "You looked it up online," he said. Pietro nodded. Karl got up, poured him a glass of warm milk and sat down beside him. "Remember what Ruggeri said in Malta?" he asked. "Data isn't proof. Online you only find data, and often not even that. Don't trust the first look. You need someone who knows how to really look." Pietro drank the milk. "A doctor," he said. "A doctor," Karl confirmed. "The problem is getting her there."

That evening a council of war was held on the first floor, in Matei and Giulia's kitchen, while Graziella served dinners downstairs, unaware of everything. There were Pietro, Karl, Matei, Giulia, Chiara, and Bellini, who climbed the stairs with difficulty but insisted on being there. The problem was simple to describe and impossible to solve: Graziella would never go to the doctor. In fifty years she had never been, except for vaccinations and to accompany others. She said doctors always find something, if you let them look, and that she had no time to be ill. "If we ask her, she'll take it badly," said Giulia. "She'll say we're treating her like an old woman." Bellini, who had kept quiet until then, raised a hand. "Leave it to me," he said. "Graziella and I have the same heart. The same doctor. And the same pride. I know how to convince a stubborn mule."

Viola, who should have been asleep, had heard everything from her bedroom door, in her pyjamas, with her teddy bear in her arms. When she saw her, Giulia picked her up and explained, in simple words, that Granny Graziella's heart was a bit tired, and that a doctor would help her. Viola listened with the utmost seriousness. Then she asked whether a tired heart could be restored, like paintings. Giulia hesitated. "More or less," she said. "There's a doctor who cleans it, the way Chiara cleans panels." Viola seemed satisfied. She went back to her room and, instead of sleeping, began to draw. The next day, on the trattoria kitchen table, Graziella found a sheet: a big red heart with a plaster on it, and next to it a little man in a white coat with a brush in his hand. Underneath, Viola had written in the crooked letters she had just learned: "FOR GRANY GRAZIELA. THE DOCTER RESTORES." Graziella pinned it above the stove, next to the rules.

Bellini's plan was simple and a little dishonest, as he himself admitted. The following Monday, at eleven, when the trattoria was quiet, he came into the kitchen with his stick and sat on Graziella's stool, with the face of someone with bad news. He said he had a cardiologist's appointment the next day, for a check-up, and that he was afraid to go alone. He said Rita worked nights, that Matei and Giulia had a restoration, that Chiara was in Siena. "Would you come with me?" he asked. Graziella looked at him for a long time, with narrowed eyes. "You're afraid of doctors?" she asked. "Since when?" "Since I turned sixty-five with a stent in my heart," replied Bellini. Graziella sighed, wiped her hands on her apron and said yes. It was the first time in fifty years anyone had asked her to go with them to a doctor. She couldn't refuse.

The cardiologist was Dr Neri, the councillor's cousin, a man of sixty with big, calm hands, who had known Bellini for ten years and who had been warned by Pietro, in an email written in perfect formal Italian: "Dear Doctor, I take the liberty of drawing to your attention…". He examined Bellini for five minutes, said he was very well, then turned to Graziella, who was waiting on a chair in a corner, her bag on her knees. "And you, signora?" he asked, as if it had only just occurred to him. "Since you're here, shall we have a quick listen?" Graziella understood everything in a second. She looked at Bellini, who was looking at the ceiling with exaggerated innocence. For a long moment it seemed she would get up and leave. Then she took off her coat, slowly. "All right," she said. "But only because I'm here anyway. And because this old swindler will pay for it."

The examination lasted an hour. Electrocardiogram, blood pressure, an ultrasound of the heart, a long series of questions which Graziella answered in monosyllables. Bellini waited in the corridor, sitting on a plastic chair, his stick between his knees, now and then looking at his watch. When the door opened, Dr Neri came out first. He wasn't smiling. He told Bellini he needed to speak to the lady's family, and Bellini replied that he was the family, for today, and that the others would arrive in ten minutes. Then the doctor explained, in simple words. One of the arteries carrying blood to the heart was almost blocked. That was why she was short of breath, why she got tired, why she felt that weight on her chest. It wasn't an emergency, not yet. But she needed an operation. Soon. "A bypass," said the doctor. "It's an operation we do every day. But at seventy-five you don't put it off."

While waiting for the others to arrive, Bellini stayed alone in the corridor, his stick between his knees, and remembered another corridor, three years earlier, when it was he who sat on that plastic chair, with the same fear in his stomach, on the morning of the stent. Back then nobody had asked to go with him. He had gone alone, out of pride. And when he came out of the theatre, dazed and weak, the first person he saw in the corridor was Graziella, with a thermos under her arm and an angry face. "Did you think you'd manage on your own?" she had said. "Stubborn as a mule." In the thermos was ribollita. He had eaten it in a hospital bed, with a plastic spoon, and it had been the best ribollita of his life. Now, three years later, it was his turn. Bellini got up, went to the coffee machine and got two. One for himself. One for someone as stubborn as a mule.

Graziella came out of the consulting room with her coat already on and her bag under her arm, as if she were going to the market. She looked at Bellini, who had stood up leaning on his stick. "You tricked me," she said. "In fifty years nobody's ever tricked me." Bellini didn't answer. She was silent for a moment, then added, more quietly: "Thank you." It was the first time, in all the years they had known each other, that Bellini heard her say thank you to anyone without a plate in her hand. Then Graziella set off towards the exit, with her usual determined step, and stopped only at the lift. "The doctor says May," she said without turning round. "I say after the neighbourhood festival. Ribollita for three hundred people doesn't make itself." Bellini smiled for the first time all morning. "We'll talk about it," he said. "Calmly." "There's nothing to talk about," replied Graziella. And she pressed the button.

They did talk about it, though, that very evening, at the trattoria, behind closed doors, all round the big table. Graziella sat at the head, arms folded, like a besieged general. The neighbourhood festival was at the end of June: waiting meant another two months with an artery almost blocked. Dr Neri, on the phone, had been clear: it wasn't prudent. Graziella had been just as clear: the trattoria wouldn't close, not even for a day, not even for her heart. It was Pietro who found the solution, or at least the beginning of one. "Grandma," he said, "we're not asking you to close the trattoria. We're asking you to leave it to us for a month." Graziella looked at him as if he had blasphemed. "To you?" she said. "Which of you can make ribollita?" There was a silence. Then Karl raised his hand, slowly, as at school. "Me," he said. "Ninety-eight per cent."

Graziella looked at Karl for a long time. Then she looked at the others, one by one. Matei, who could make his mother's sarmale but had never lit the trattoria stove. Giulia, who cooked pasta alla sorrentina beautifully and nothing else. Chiara, who could burn water. Pietro, who had been waiting on tables since he was eight. Bellini, who had never cooked in his life, and said so proudly. "You're a disaster," she said at last. "A restorers' cooperative wanting to run a trattoria. My father would turn in his grave." But her voice wasn't angry. It was tired, and a little moved. "All right," she said after a long silence. "I'll have the operation in May. But on one condition. For the next three weeks, Karl comes here every morning at five, not six. And learns the rest. All of it. Except the two per cent."

Later that evening Marco arrived, Pietro's father, who worked at Careggi hospital and had heard everything from Giulia on the phone. He came into the trattoria still with his hospital badge round his neck and stopped in front of his mother. He didn't greet her. "You hid it from me," he said. "I've worked in a hospital for thirty years and my mother hides from me that she has heart trouble." Graziella didn't answer. Marco was upset for a good ten minutes, pacing up and down between the tables, while everyone pretended not to listen. Then he stopped, sat down next to her and took her hand. "Why didn't you tell me?" he asked, more quietly. Graziella looked at her hand in her son's. "Because you're my son," she said. "Children mustn't worry about their mothers. It's the other way round." Marco shook his head and laughed, his eyes moist. "Mum," he said, "I'm over fifty." "Exactly," replied Graziella. "You're still little."

From that day on everyone rolled up their sleeves. Karl arrived at five, his eyes still closed, and left at eleven, his hands smelling of onion, to run to the workshop and finish the thesis he was working on with Ruggeri. Pietro started studying the trattoria accounts, the squared notebook from 1974, and discovered that his grandmother knew by heart the price of every supplier for the last ten years. Matei and Giulia organised the shifts, written on a blackboard in the kitchen, like a restoration plan. Chiara offered to do the till, because at least with numbers she couldn't burn anything. Davide drew a sign for the door: "Graziella is resting. The trattoria isn't." And Valeria, when she heard, turned up one Saturday morning in an apron and said a neighbourhood councillor could wash dishes too, now and then. Nobody had the courage to say no.

The neighbourhood, too, got busy when it heard. The news passed from mouth to mouth in one afternoon, from the fruit seller to the baker, from the baker to the bar, from the bar to the shoemaker's. Guido turned up the next day with a pair of soft leather slippers, made by him, for the hospital: "So at least in there you'll walk properly." The fruit seller promised the best vegetables at half price for the whole month, "and woe betide anyone who tells". Old Signor Franco, ninety, said he would come on Thursdays anyway, even without Graziella, "to make sure the kids don't ruin the tripe". Efisio offered to peel the potatoes, and really did, every morning, sitting on a crate in front of the kitchen door, singing the songs of his village under his breath. Graziella, who saw everything from the window, grumbled that she wasn't dead yet. But in the evening, when nobody was looking, she wiped her eyes with her apron.

The morning lessons changed in nature. Graziella no longer taught only ribollita: she taught everything. Pappa al pomodoro, Thursday's tripe, Sunday broth, grandma's cake, how to talk to the fishmonger and how to ask the baker for yesterday's bread. She taught the things that weren't written anywhere: which customer wanted his soup boiling and which lukewarm, which old gentleman had to be brought his coffee without asking, why the table by the window was never given to tourists on Friday evenings. Karl wrote everything in his notebook. By the end of the second week the notebook was full, and Karl bought a second one. On the cover Graziella wrote, in red marker: "Things that aren't said. Volume two." Then she added, below, smaller: "Volume one is in my head. That one I'm not giving you."

One morning, at the end of the third week, Karl made the ribollita on his own, from start to finish, while Graziella watched him from the stool, without saying a word. He made the soffritto without garlic. He cut the black cabbage into thin strips. He added the beans, half whole and half puréed. He added the stale bread, the water, the salt, "as much as needed". He left the pot to rest all night, and the next morning boiled it again, as the name says. When it was ready, he filled a bowl, poured a thread of new oil over it and handed it to Graziella. She tasted a spoonful. Then another. Then she put down the spoon and sat in silence, looking at the bowl. Karl waited, his heart pounding as before an exam board. "Ninety-eight," Graziella said at last. "Maybe ninety-nine." Then she got up, went to the pantry, took a jar without a label and hid it in her pocket. "The rest," she said, "when I come back."

That evening Graziella did something she had never done. She called Pietro into her bedroom, where nobody ever went, and showed him a drawer of the chest. Inside were things nobody had ever seen: the trattoria's first licence, from 1950, signed by her father; Aldo's letters, tied with a red ribbon; a photograph of her at twelve, in the mud of 1966, with a tray of sandwiches in her hand; the savings book opened for Pietro on the day he was born. "If it goes badly in May," said Graziella, in the most normal voice in the world, "everything is here. Your father knows where the papers are. But the important things you need to know." Pietro felt his throat tighten. "Grandma," he said, "it won't go badly." Graziella closed the drawer. "I know," she said. "But restorers always say that before an intervention you do the documentation. This is mine."

Before going to sleep, Pietro opened the black notebook and wrote the date. Then, for the first time since he had kept it, he couldn't write anything for a long moment. In the end he wrote a list, as Karl had done. "Things I've learned this month. One: you can feel at home in a kitchen even if you can't cook. Two: people who say 'I'm perfectly fine' too quickly usually aren't. Three: you mustn't take it badly when someone looks at you too closely; they just love you. Four: grandmothers are afraid too. Only they put it in the soffritto, together with the onion, and nobody sees it." He reread the list, then added a fifth line, the shortest. "Five: in May I won't be wrong. I'll be there watching. And she'll be fine." He underlined it twice, the way you underline a promise.
Qual è la terza regola di Graziella?
La ribollita non si inventa, si impara
Che cosa ha notato Karl nella quarta settimana?
Che Graziella si stancava e si teneva una mano sul petto
Come ha convinto Bellini Graziella ad andare dal medico?

Che cosa ha detto il dottor Neri?
Che bisogna operare presto con un bypass
Che deve smettere di cucinare per sempre
Che voto dà Graziella alla ribollita di Karl?
Don't take it badly with him.
I get on well with my colleagues.
He finally made up his mind to speak.
